title: Strategy Foundations
content: Strategy is choosing where to play and how to win for sustainable advantage. It's about trade-offs — deciding what NOT to do. KEY CONCEPTS: Strategy answers what business you're in, who your customers are, and why you win. WORKED EXAMPLE: A budget airline wins by choosing NOT to offer frills — focus creates advantage. PRACTICE: 1) State your where-to-play. 2) State your how-to-win. 3) List what you'll deliberately NOT do.
quiz_json: [{"q": "Strategy is fundamentally about:", "options": ["Doing everything", "Trade-offs \u2014 what NOT to do", "Copying rivals", "Lowest price always"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Strategy means deliberate trade-offs."}, {"q": "Sustainable advantage comes from:", "options": ["Luck", "Choices about where to play and how to win", "Ads", "Size alone"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Where-to-play + how-to-win."}, {"q": "A budget airline dropping frills shows:", "options": ["Weakness", "Focus creating advantage", "Poor service strategy", "Randomness"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Deliberate focus creates advantage."}]

title: Porter's Five Forces
content: Industry profit potential is shaped by five forces: new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, substitutes, rivalry. KEY CONCEPTS: Strong forces compress margins; weak forces enable profit. Position where forces are weakest. WORKED EXAMPLE: A patent (barrier to entry) weakens the new-entrant threat, protecting margin. PRACTICE: 1) Score each force in your industry. 2) Identify the strongest threat. 3) Plan to weaken it.

title: Competitive Advantage
content: Porter's generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, or focus. Being 'stuck in the middle' is fatal. KEY CONCEPTS: Be the cheapest OR the most distinctive, not neither. Focus dominates a niche. WORKED EXAMPLE: A premium brand charges 3x by being unmistakably different, not slightly better. PRACTICE: 1) Pick your generic strategy. 2) Prove you're not stuck in the middle. 3) Define your edge.
quiz_json: [{"q": "According to Porter's generic strategies, which approach is NOT recommended for achieving competitive advantage?", "options": ["Cost leadership", "Differentiation", "Focus", "Being 'stuck in the middle'"], "correct": 3, "explanation": "Being 'stuck in the middle' means failing to commit to either cost leadership, differentiation, or focus, which is considered fatal for competitive advantage."}, {"q": "What does the 'focus' strategy primarily emphasize?", "options": ["Competing on the lowest cost across the entire market", "Serving a specific niche with either cost leadership or differentiation", "Offering a product slightly better than competitors", "Charging premium prices without clear differentiation"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "The focus strategy targets a specific niche, dominating it through either cost leadership or differentiation."}, {"q": "In the worked example, why does a premium brand charge three times more than competitors?", "options": ["Because it is slightly better than competitors", "Because it is unmistakably different and distinctive", "Because it uses a focus strategy on a niche", "Because it is the cheapest in the market"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "The premium brand charges a higher price by being unmistakably different, not just slightly better, demonstrating differentiation."}]

title: SWOT & Positioning
content: SWOT: internal Strengths/Weaknesses, external Opportunities/Threats. Position where strengths meet opportunity and rivals are weak. KEY CONCEPTS: Be different, not just better — own a distinct place in the customer's mind. WORKED EXAMPLE: A challenger positions as 'the simple alternative' where incumbents are complex. PRACTICE: 1) Complete a SWOT. 2) Find your distinct position. 3) Name the rival weakness you exploit.

title: Value Chain & Moats
content: Value chain maps every value-adding activity. Economic moats (Buffett) protect profit: network effects, switching costs, cost advantage, brand, scale. KEY CONCEPTS: Advantage comes from doing key activities better or cheaper. Durability matters most. WORKED EXAMPLE: A marketplace's network effect deepens its moat with every new user. PRACTICE: 1) Map your value chain. 2) Identify your moat type. 3) Plan to widen it.

title: Blue Ocean & Growth
content: Blue Ocean: create uncontested market space via value innovation (differentiation + low cost). Ansoff matrix guides growth. KEY CONCEPTS: Make competition irrelevant by redefining the market. Eliminate-reduce-raise-create. WORKED EXAMPLE: Cirque du Soleil dropped animals/stars (cost) and added artistry (value) — a new category. PRACTICE: 1) List industry factors to eliminate/reduce. 2) List factors to raise/create. 3) Sketch your blue ocean.

title: Grandmaster — Business Models & Execution
content: Design how you create, deliver, capture value. Strategy without execution is hallucination. KEY CONCEPTS: Align structure, incentives, culture to strategy. OKRs cascade goals; Balanced Scorecard tracks performance. WORKED EXAMPLE: A subscription model turns one-time sales into recurring revenue and higher valuation. PRACTICE: 1) Map your business model. 2) Set 3 OKRs. 3) Align one incentive to strategy.

title: King Level — Shaping Industries
content: At King level you shape industry-level moves and create categories. KEY CONCEPTS: Set the rules others follow. Build platforms and ecosystems, not just products. Anticipate and drive disruption before it hits you. WORKED EXAMPLE: A platform company turns competitors into partners on its ecosystem, controlling the market. PRACTICE: 1) Envision your industry in 5 years. 2) Define the rule you want to set. 3) Design an ecosystem play.
